Grazia (1919-2014) was the son of Italian immigrants who moved to Chicago in order to escape political drama in his father's home town of Licodia in Sicily. Grazia attended the University of Chicago and Columbia University, before earning a PhD back at the University of Chicago in political science. He served in WW2 as a captain, and participated in campaigns in North Africa, Italy, France, and Germany. According to the Wikipedia article on him, he "specialized in mechanized warfare, intelligence and psychological warfare." The last of these, psychological warfare, is perhaps of particular interest given his support of Velikovsky, a Russian Jew who has always been a controversial figure, even within revisionist circles.

On October 31, 2014, he posthumously made a Distinguished Member of the Regiment of Psychological Operations of the Special Operations Command at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.[15]"

Grazia was also involved in politics and wrote widely-acclaimed books on political science. His political positions lean toward leftism, but not quite as it manifests today, being from an earlier generation. He was critical of the amount of power wielded by the presidency, and emphasized the role that bureaucracies and committees play in the decision-making process of government. Later, he returned to Europe to found an experimental and socially liberal school in Switzerland. He invited the Beat poet William S. Burroughs to teach there, and, as might be expected, attracted mostly a bunch of hippies. Near the end of his life he traveled around internationally to teach at various other universities from Istanbul to Bombay, and died in 2014.

A collection of Oswald Spenger's work in the original German can be found here: http://www.zeno.org/Philosophie/M/Spengler,+Oswald

Spengler (1880-1936) was mostly active during the interwar period in Germany, in the 1920s and 30s, and died in 1936. He wrote on a variety of subjects, including historical chronology. He believed that historical time, especially for prehistoric cultures, had been grossly exaggerated in many cases, including in the Americas. He argued, very reasonably, that massive social and even civilizational changes could take place within as little as a single generation, and that it was not necessary to imagine centuries of elapsed time in order to explain migrations or other events reflected in archaeological data.

He published a piece in 1933 titled Das Alter der amerikanischen Kulturen, in which he argued that the western coast of South America was colonized by people who crossed the Pacific Ocean within the last 2000 years. He pointed out similarities in architecture, tattooing practices, and other cultural manifestations between prehistoric American cultures and old Japan, Malaysia, and the Dravidians in India, for example. Again, he did not believe that many centuries were required to explain this diffusion, arguing that it could have easily taken place within only a few generations' time, and using old Japanese culture as a sort of chronological anchoring point for South American colonization.

Besides such historical and chronological revisions, Spengler is best remembered for his work Der Untergang des Abendlandes, or The Decline of the West, where he compares civilizational culture to a superorganism that has a finite lifespan just like any other living organism. Spengler rejected National Socialism because of its racial emphasis, and looked to Benito Mussolini as a role model instead. Spengler believed that a strong executive power would become necessary by around the year 2000 in order to counter the crises created by the collapse of western civilization.
Oswald Spenger, German philosopher and historian

Jean Hardouin (1646–1729)was a French scholar who lived from 1646 to 1729. He was born in Brittany but moved to Paris where he joined the Jesuit order at 16 years old. He was interested in numismatics and published works contending that several important classical works were medieval forgeries of the 13th century, produced by monks under the direction of Severus Archontius.

Two of his works on chronology were published under the titles of Chronologiae ex nummis antiquis restitutae (1696) and Prolegomena ad censuram veterum scriptorum (1729). In these volumes, Hardouin argues that works of Homer, Herodotus, Cicero, Pliny, Virgil, and Horace, among others, were all fabricated by Catholic scribes at other monasteries. He also questioned the authenticity of works of art said to be ancient, as well as inscriptions and the allegedly ancient coins of his numismatic studies. He found further chronological issues in Dante's work.

His Prolegomena was his last work, coincidentally published within the same year that he died, and in it he made arguments that the New Testament was originally composed in Latin.

The following works of Hardouin are available at Archive.org:

Prolegomena ad censuram veterum scriptorum (Introduction to the Censorship of Former Writers, 1766, in Latin)

Chronologiae ex nummis antiquis restitutae (Chronology of Ancient Coins of Herodian, 1693, in Latin)

Antirrheticus de nummis antiquis coloniarum et municipiorum (Cash from the Old Colonies, 1689, Latin)

Doutes proposés sur l'age du Dante (Proposed Doubts on the Age of Dante, in French, 1847 edition)
